question: What is the basic structural and functional unit of all living things?
explanation: The cell is recognized universally as the fundamental building block that makes up all structures and performs all basic functions in living organisms. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T9#GNS111_U1_T9_h1)

question: When two or more different tissue types team up to do a specific job, what level of body organization do they form?
explanation: You've got it! An organ is simply a structure made of different tissues working together—like your heart or stomach. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T9#GNS111_U1_T9_h1)

question: Which body system mops up leaked fluids and helps defend you against infections?
explanation: Well done! The lymphatic system acts like the body's drainage and defense network, filtering fluid and fighting off germs. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T9#GNS111_U1_T9_h2)

question: Which system works closely with the nervous system to control body activities using chemical messengers?
explanation: Spot on! The endocrine system sends out hormones to regulate your body over time, teaming up with your nerves to keep things running smoothly. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T9#GNS111_U1_T9_h2)

question: What is one of the main jobs of the liver in our body?

options.C: Pumping oxygenated blood to the brain
options.D: Producing insulin to lower blood glucose

explanation: Correct! The liver is a busy chemical factory: it cleans our blood of toxins and builds essential proteins. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T9#GNS111_U1_T9_h3)

question: A patient with kidney failure has fluid overload and waste buildup. What is the normal job of healthy kidneys?

options.B: Red blood cell production in the bone marrow

explanation: You nailed it! Kidneys act like high-tech filters, clearing out waste and extra water to keep your body clean and balanced. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T9#GNS111_U1_T9_h3)

question: What do we call the body's ability to keep its internal environment steady and balanced?
explanation: Spot on! Homeostasis is all about balance—keeping your internal conditions stable no matter what's happening outside. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T9#GNS111_U1_T9_h4)

question: How do negative feedback loops help protect the body when things start going out of whack?

options.A: By reversing a deviation away from a normal set point
options.B: By replacing damaged cells with scar tissue
options.C: By shutting down organ systems to conserve energy
options.D: By amplifying the original stimulus until an event ends

explanation: Great job! Negative feedback acts like a thermostat, pushing things back toward normal when they get too high or too low. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T9#GNS111_U1_T9_h4)

question: A patient looks pale, feels tired, and is short of breath. Why must a nurse look at the whole picture instead of just checking the lungs?

options.A: Skin color changes are completely unrelated to internal organ status
options.B: Respiratory diseases are always contagious in hospital settings
options.C: Organ systems are interdependent and rely on each other to function
options.D: Vital signs only reflect the current state of the nervous system

explanation: Spot on! Our body systems don't work in isolation; when one struggles, others (like the heart, lungs, and blood) feel the impact too. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T9#GNS111_U1_T9_h5)

question: Why are routine vital sign checks such a helpful way to assess a patient's stability?

options.A: They confirm that the patient has consumed enough water that day
options.B: They measure parameters controlled by interacting organ systems to keep the body stable
options.C: They show the exact number of active white blood cells in circulation
options.D: They measure the total amount of muscle mass in the limbs

explanation: You got it! Vitals give us a quick window into how well major systems like the heart, lungs, and nervous system are cooperating to keep the patient safe. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T9#GNS111_U1_T9_h5)
